title: Atrial fibrillation and anticoagulation
blurb: Detect atrial fibrillation, score stroke and bleeding risk with CHA2DS2-VASc and ORBIT, and support safe DOAC anticoagulation and rate control.
question: Mrs Wright, 81, has newly confirmed atrial fibrillation, hypertension and two falls this year. Her daughter asks whether she is 'too old and wobbly' for a blood thinner and whether aspirin would be safer. What does NICE NG196 say?

teach.body: Formally: atrial fibrillation is an irregular, often rapid heart rhythm in which the atria quiver rather than contract, so blood can pool and clot in the left atrium; a clot reaching the brain causes a stroke. In plain English: AF is a common, often silent cause of stroke, and anticoagulation substantially reduces that risk. The nurse's jobs: detect it, help assess risk, support safe anticoagulation and monitor rate.

steps.label: Symptoms or signs
steps.sub: breathless, palpitations, syncope, dizziness, chest discomfort, stroke/TIA

teach.caption: An irregular pulse also means automated BP devices may be inaccurate: measure BP manually (NG136 1.1.2).

head: CHA2DS2-VASc
NG196 action
teach.caption: DOACs: apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, rivaroxaban. A vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) if DOACs are contraindicated, not tolerated or unsuitable.

teach.h: Bleeding risk informs, it does not forbid
teach.body: NG196 recommends the ORBIT score to assess bleeding risk (preferred over HAS-BLED because it is better calibrated). Bleeding risk is used to discuss benefits and harms and to address modifiable risk factors, such as uncontrolled hypertension, excess alcohol or unnecessary antiplatelets. Crucially, NICE says do not withhold anticoagulation solely because of a person's age or their risk of falls.

rows.label: Rhythm control instead
rows.tag: reversible cause, new onset, HF caused by AF

teach.note: With heart failure, follow NG106: beta-blockers, and avoid rate-limiting CCBs in HFrEF. Life-threatening instability from new AF: emergency electrical cardioversion without delaying for anticoagulation (1.8.1).

items: Review the need for and quality of anticoagulation at least annually, including renal function for DOACs.
Warfarin: calculate time in therapeutic range (TTR); reassess if TTR below 65%, 2 INRs above 5 or 1 above 8 in 6 months, or 2 INRs below 1.5.
For poor control, look at cognition, adherence, illness, interacting drugs and lifestyle including diet and alcohol.
Not anticoagulated: review stroke risk at 65 or if diabetes, heart failure, PAD, CHD, stroke/TIA develops.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mrs Wright in an anticoagulation clinic
teach.body: Mrs Wright scores 3 on CHA2DS2-VASc (age 75+ = 2, hypertension = 1) plus 1 for female sex: 4. Nurse Kofi explains that NG196 offers a DOAC at a score of 2 or above, that age and falls alone are not reasons to withhold it, and that aspirin alone is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF. He completes an ORBIT bleeding assessment, reviews her falls risks and BP, and helps her and her daughter weigh up the options.

teach.text: Score trap: age 75 or over scores 2, not 1, and a previous stroke or TIA also scores 2. Women under 65 with no other risk factor score 1 for sex alone, and NG196 does NOT offer them anticoagulation. Bleeding tool: ORBIT is preferred over HAS-BLED.

items: Suspect AF: feel the pulse; confirm with a 12-lead ECG.
CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk; ORBIT for bleeding risk.
Score 2+: offer a DOAC; men scoring 1: consider; sex as the only factor under 65: do not offer.
Do not withhold for age or falls alone; no aspirin monotherapy for stroke prevention.
Rate control first-line for most: beta-blocker (not sotalol) or diltiazem/verapamil; review anticoagulation yearly.

summary: You can now detect AF, calculate CHA2DS2-VASc, and apply NG196 rules on who is offered a DOAC, including that age and falls are not reasons to withhold anticoagulation and that aspirin is not a substitute. You also know the role of ORBIT, rate control choices and how anticoagulation is kept safe.

A.q: A man has an irregular pulse on manual palpation. What does NG196 recommend to confirm atrial fibrillation?
A.why: NG196 1.1.2: perform a 12-lead ECG to confirm the diagnosis in people with an irregular pulse when AF is suspected.

whyNot.0: BP monitoring does not diagnose AF, and automated devices are unreliable with AF.
whyNot.2: A chest X-ray does not show the heart rhythm.
whyNot.3: Troponin is for suspected myocardial injury, not rhythm diagnosis.

A.q: Which tool does NG196 recommend for assessing bleeding risk before anticoagulation in AF?
A.why: NG196 1.2.2: use the ORBIT bleeding risk score, which evidence showed has better accuracy than HAS-BLED.

whyNot.0: HAS-BLED was previously used but NG196 prefers ORBIT.
whyNot.1: CHA2DS2-VASc assesses stroke risk, not bleeding.
whyNot.2: ABCD2 is a TIA score that NICE no longer recommends.

A.q: A 70-year-old man with AF has hypertension and diabetes. What is his CHA2DS2-VASc score?

whyNot.0: 2 misses one of the three risk factors.
whyNot.1: 4 would need another factor, such as age 75 or over.
whyNot.3: 5 counts factors he does not have.

B.q: A woman, 58, has AF and no risk factors other than her sex (CHA2DS2-VASc 1). What does NG196 advise about anticoagulation?
B.why: NG196 1.6.7: do not offer anticoagulation to people under 65 with AF and no risk factors other than sex (score 0 for men, 1 for women).

whyNot.1: A DOAC is offered at a score of 2 or more (excluding sex alone at this age).
whyNot.2: Warfarin is not indicated with this very low risk.
whyNot.3: Aspirin monotherapy is not offered for stroke prevention in AF.

B.q: A GP suggests aspirin for stroke prevention in a man with AF who is anxious about bleeding. What does NG196 say?
options: Aspirin plus warfarin is the safest
B.why: NG196 1.6.14: do not offer aspirin monotherapy solely for stroke prevention to people with AF.

whyNot.0: Aspirin is not an alternative to anticoagulation for AF stroke prevention.
whyNot.1: Age does not make aspirin the preferred option.
whyNot.3: Combining them increases bleeding and is not the recommended approach.

B.q: Which drug does NG196 recommend as first-line rate control for a man with permanent AF and no heart failure?
B.why: Bisoprolol is a standard beta-blocker. NG196 1.7.2: offer a standard beta-blocker (not sotalol) or a rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem or verapamil) as initial rate-control monotherapy.

whyNot.1: Sotalol is excluded from the 'standard beta-blocker' choice.
whyNot.2: Amiodarone is a rhythm-control drug, not first-line rate control.
whyNot.3: Flecainide is used for rhythm control.

C.q: Mr Turner, 79, with AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc of 4, fell twice last year. His son asks the nurse to cancel the planned DOAC because of the falls. What is the best response?
options: Agree, as falls make DOACs unsafe for him
Explain falls do not justify withholding
Suggest aspirin as a safer option
Suggest waiting until he is 80 to start
C.why: NG196 1.6.8: do not withhold anticoagulation solely because of age or falls risk. Discuss benefits and harms, assess bleeding risk with ORBIT and address falls risk factors.

whyNot.0: Falls risk alone is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation.
whyNot.2: Aspirin monotherapy is not offered for AF stroke prevention.
whyNot.3: Delay leaves him at stroke risk without benefit.

C.q: Mrs Ndlovu, 72, on warfarin for AF, has had INRs of 5.4 and 6.1 in the last 6 months. What does NG196 advise?
options: Continue and recheck INR in 3 months
C.why: NG196 1.6.11: reassess anticoagulation if control is poor, including 2 INR values above 5 (or 1 above 8) within 6 months, and address causes such as adherence, illness and interacting drugs.

whyNot.0: Two INRs above 5 mean poor control needing reassessment now.
whyNot.2: Aspirin monotherapy is not offered for stroke prevention.
whyNot.3: Less frequent testing would worsen safety.

C.q: A man with AF that started this morning arrives with a heart rate of 170, BP 72/40 and new confusion. What does NG196 recommend?
options: Oral bisoprolol and review in an hour
Digoxin orally and a repeat ECG
C.why: NG196 1.8.1: for life-threatening haemodynamic instability caused by new-onset AF, perform emergency electrical cardioversion without delaying to achieve anticoagulation.

whyNot.0: Oral rate control is too slow in life-threatening instability.
whyNot.1: Cardioversion is not delayed to start anticoagulation in this situation.
whyNot.3: Oral digoxin is too slow and inappropriate here.

reteach.title: Stroke risk outweighs most fears
reteach.question: Why does NICE push so hard against withholding anticoagulation in older people who fall?

blocks.body: Every person with AF has a stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) and a bleeding risk (ORBIT). Age raises both, so 'too old' often means 'highest benefit'. A fall is frightening, but the stroke risk from untreated AF is usually far greater than the bleeding risk from falls. So NICE says: do not withhold for age or falls alone. Instead reduce what you can (falls risks, BP, alcohol, unnecessary antiplatelets) and decide together.

blocks.text: A high bleeding score is a prompt to address modifiable risks and discuss, not an automatic 'no'.

explain.body: Manual pulse palpation in anyone with breathlessness, palpitations, syncope, dizziness, chest discomfort or stroke/TIA. Confirm with a 12-lead ECG.

test.q: A woman presents with dizziness and palpitations. What is the first step to detect possible AF?
test.why: NG196 1.1.1: perform manual pulse palpation to assess for an irregular pulse in people with symptoms suggesting AF.

whyNot.0: Echo assesses structure later, not first detection.
whyNot.2: Ambulatory monitoring is for suspected paroxysmal AF not caught on ECG.
whyNot.3: Thyroid tests look for a cause, not detection.

explain.body: CHA2DS2-VASc: CHF 1, hypertension 1, age 75+ 2, diabetes 1, stroke/TIA/thromboembolism 2, vascular disease 1, age 65–74 1, female 1.

test.q: A 66-year-old woman with AF had a TIA last year. What is her CHA2DS2-VASc score?

whyNot.0: 2 counts the TIA but misses age and sex.
whyNot.3: 5 adds a factor she does not have.

explain.body: Score 2 or more: offer a DOAC. Men scoring 1: consider. Under 65 with sex as the only factor: do not offer. Warfarin if DOACs unsuitable. Do not withhold for age or falls.

test.q: Which of these is a DOAC?
test.why: DOACs in NG196 are apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban and rivaroxaban.

whyNot.0: Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist.
whyNot.2: Enoxaparin is a low molecular weight heparin.

explain.body: Rate control first-line for most: standard beta-blocker (not sotalol) or diltiazem/verapamil; digoxin if sedentary. Review anticoagulation at least yearly, including renal function on DOACs.

test.q: How often does NG196 advise reviewing anticoagulation in a stable person with AF on a DOAC?
test.why: NG196 1.6.17: review the need for and quality of anticoagulation at least annually (including renal function for DOACs), or more often if relevant events occur.

whyNot.0: Five years is far too long.
whyNot.2: Reviews are scheduled, not left to symptom changes.
